title: The Third Column of Work
author: Braincentric
summary: The piece argues that career advancement has always run on two unstated columns -- Hard Skills (what got you hired) and Soft Skills (what got you promoted) -- and that AI is now visibly draining the first column while exposing the need for a third: 'Stake Skills,' the practices that let a person credibly own and answer for work a machine helped produce. Using a fictionalized scene of a worker named Aaron getting a panicked call from her boss after an AI-drafted proposal contains an error, the author argues that 'the AI drafted it' functions exactly like the old excuse 'I didn't check it' -- nobody on the other end of the accountability chain cares what produced the mistake, only who signed off on it. The piece connects this to the older, mostly hidden practice of 'CYA' (covering your ass), arguing Stake Skills simply take that same instinct and turn it to face forward: keeping an open, proactive record of what a person verified and why, before anything goes wrong. As proof of concept, the piece includes a real, dated production log of its own writing process, showing exactly where a human made judgment calls, overruled AI suggestions, and caught factual errors.
points: Names a third career 'column' beyond Hard Skills (what gets you hired) and Soft Skills (what gets you promoted): Stake Skills -- the practices that let a person credibly own and answer for work a machine helped produce.
Uses a factory-floor-style anecdote (a worker's boss asking 'did you check this?' after an AI-drafted proposal contains an error) to argue 'the AI drafted it' has zero defensive value.

Reframes 'CYA' (covering your ass) as an instinct people already have but practice backwards -- a hidden trail built defensively after something goes wrong -- arguing Stake Skills is the same instinct turned proactive and visible.
Backs the argument with its own dated production log showing exactly where the human author made judgment calls, refused AI-drafted material, and caught the AI's factual errors.
quotes: Hard Skills got you hired. Soft Skills got you promoted. The third column is Stake Skills. They keep you in the room.

You don't have to be a learning scientist to know what happens when that sentence enters the room. It does nothing. It has never worked, anywhere, one time. The boss doesn't care what drafted the thing.

This is taking that covered ass and turning it to face front. Same instinctual muscle. Same record that used to be in the shadows. But now you keep it on purpose, in the open, before anything goes wrong, instead of in secret for after it does.
A record only works when somebody has agreed to answer for it. I do below.
We all know producing got cheap. Answering for the thing did not. A machine can now fill column one (Hard Skills) faster than you ever could. It cannot touch column three (Stake Skills).
